title: How Many Drinks to Get Drunk? BAC by Weight, Sex, and Pace
excerpt: How many drinks it takes to feel tipsy or reach 0.08% BAC, by weight and sex, plus the factors that change your number and how to pace a night out safely.
metaDescription: How many drinks to get drunk? Estimates by weight and sex, what counts as one drink, why BAC keeps rising, and how to pace yourself safely.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how many drinks to get drunk
content:
**The honest answer first:** for an average adult drinking at a normal pace, it takes roughly **2 to 3 standard drinks to feel tipsy** and roughly **3 to 5 standard drinks within about two hours to reach a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.08%**, the US legal driving limit and the level most people would call "drunk." A smaller person, a woman, someone drinking on an empty stomach, or someone drinking fast can get there on fewer. A larger person who eats and paces can take more. There's no single number, and that's the most useful thing to understand about it.

This guide is written for adults of legal drinking age who want to know where their limits are so they can **stay on the comfortable side of them**. It isn't a guide to getting drunk faster. The point of knowing the numbers is pacing: enjoying a night out, staying in control, getting home safely, and waking up without a brutal hangover.

> **Safety first.** No drink count makes it safe to drive. Impairment starts well below 0.08%, and the only safe BAC for driving is zero. **Call 911 right away if someone** can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, is vomiting while confused or passed out, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, which can be fatal. Don't leave them to "sleep it off." If you're pregnant, under 21, take medications that interact with alcohol, or have a health condition, the right number of drinks may be zero. Talk to your doctor if you're unsure.

## First, What Counts as "One Drink"?

Every drink-count answer depends on what a "drink" is, and most people underestimate this. In the US, a **standard drink** contains about **14 grams of pure alcohol** (around 0.6 fluid ounces). That's the definition used by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA). It equals roughly:

| Drink | Standard size | Typical strength |
|---|---|---|
| Regular beer | 12 oz | about 5% ABV |
| Malt liquor | 8 to 9 oz | about 7% ABV |
| Wine | 5 oz | about 12% ABV |
| Distilled spirits (vodka, whiskey, rum, tequila) | 1.5 oz shot | about 40% ABV (80 proof) |

The trouble is that real-world drinks rarely match these sizes:

- **A pint of beer is 16 oz, not 12.** A pint of a 7% IPA is closer to **2 standard drinks** than 1.
- **Restaurant and home wine pours are often 6 to 9 oz.** A big glass of wine can be 1.5 to 2 drinks, and a bottle of wine holds about 5 standard drinks.
- **Cocktails vary wildly.** A margarita, Long Island iced tea, or double whiskey can contain 2 to 3 standard drinks in one glass.
- **Hard seltzers and canned cocktails** range from about 4% to 8% or more, and cans are often 12 to 19 oz.

So when someone says "I only had three drinks," they may have had five. Counting **standard drinks**, not glasses, is the first step to knowing where you are. If you want to see how strength and size add up, our [blood alcohol calculator guide](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) walks through the math.

## How Drunk Is "Drunk"? The BAC Scale in Plain Words

"Drunk" isn't one state. It's a range, and BAC (the percentage of your blood that is alcohol) is the usual way to describe it. The effects below are general descriptions that appear in public-health and traffic-safety materials. Individual responses vary, and people with a high tolerance may feel less affected even at the same BAC.

| Approximate BAC | What it typically feels and looks like |
|---|---|
| 0.02% to 0.03% | Mild relaxation, slight warmth, a little more talkative. Judgment already slightly affected. |
| 0.04% to 0.06% | "Tipsy" or buzzed. Lowered inhibitions, louder, more confident, reduced caution. Reaction time is slower. |
| 0.07% to 0.09% | Coordination, balance, and reaction time clearly impaired. Judgment and self-control reduced. 0.08% is the legal driving limit in most of the US. |
| 0.10% to 0.12% | Obvious intoxication. Slurred speech, poor balance, slowed thinking. |
| 0.13% to 0.20% | Heavy intoxication. Blurred vision, major loss of coordination, nausea and vomiting are common. Blackouts become more likely. |
| 0.25% to 0.30% | Severe impairment, confusion, stupor. Risk of choking on vomit and of alcohol poisoning. |
| 0.30% and above | Life-threatening. Risk of losing consciousness, dangerously slowed breathing, and death. |

Most people would call 0.08% "drunk," and that's also the point where the NIAAA defines a **binge**: a pattern of drinking that brings BAC to 0.08% or higher, which typically happens after about **4 drinks for women or 5 drinks for men in about 2 hours**. That definition is a useful mental marker. If you're on pace to hit it, you've reached the point where risks start to climb quickly.

## Estimated Drinks to Reach Tipsy and Drunk, by Weight and Sex

The most widely used way to estimate BAC is the **Widmark formula**, developed in the early 20th century and still the basis of most online calculators. It uses the amount of alcohol you drank, your body weight, a factor for how much of your body is water (which differs on average between men and women), and the rate your body clears alcohol over time (commonly estimated at about 0.015% BAC per hour).

The table below shows rough Widmark estimates for how many standard drinks, spread over **about 2 hours**, it takes to reach two levels: around **0.05%** (clearly buzzed, judgment affected) and around **0.08%** (legally drunk for driving). These numbers are approximate and for an average person. Treat them as a ballpark, not a target.

| Body weight | Men: to ~0.05% | Men: to ~0.08% | Women: to ~0.05% | Women: to ~0.08% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120 lb (54 kg) | about 2 | about 3 | about 1.5 to 2 | about 2 to 2.5 |
| 150 lb (68 kg) | about 2.5 | about 3.5 | about 2 | about 3 |
| 180 lb (82 kg) | about 3 | about 4 to 4.5 | about 2.5 | about 3.5 |
| 210 lb (95 kg) | about 3.5 | about 5 | about 3 | about 4 |

A few things this table can't tell you:

- **It assumes steady drinking over 2 hours.** Drinking the same amount in 30 minutes pushes your peak much higher.
- **It assumes average absorption.** Food in your stomach can lower your peak noticeably. An empty stomach raises it.
- **Real people vary a lot.** Two people with the same weight and sex can differ meaningfully in BAC after the same drinks, because liver enzymes, body composition, and absorption all differ.
- **It says nothing about safety to drive.** Impairment begins well before 0.08%. Several studies and traffic agencies have documented reduced driving ability starting at low BACs, which is why some US states and many countries use a lower limit (Utah uses 0.05%).

For a deeper look at how long that alcohol stays in your body afterward, see our guide to [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system).

## How Many Beers to Get Drunk?

Using standard 12 oz beers at about 5% ABV, the numbers line up with the table above: an average man around 180 lb might reach 0.08% after about **4 to 5 beers in two hours**, and an average woman around 140 lb after about **3 beers in two hours**. Light beers (around 4% ABV) take a bit more. Craft beers change the picture fast:

- A 16 oz pint of a 6.5% IPA is about **1.7 standard drinks**.
- A 16 oz can of an 8% double IPA is about **2.6 standard drinks**.
- A 12 oz "imperial stout" at 10% or more is close to **2 standard drinks**.

That's why people say a few craft beers "hit harder." They do. Two pints of strong IPA can equal four or five regular beers.

## How Many Shots to Get Drunk?

A standard 1.5 oz shot of 80-proof liquor is one standard drink, so the shot numbers are the same as the drink numbers: **roughly 3 to 5 shots in two hours** for many adults to reach 0.08%. But shots carry a special risk because of **speed**. Three shots in 15 minutes don't feel like much at first, because the alcohol hasn't been absorbed yet. Twenty to sixty minutes later, BAC is still climbing. People who keep taking shots because they "don't feel it yet" are the ones most likely to overshoot into vomiting, blackouts, or alcohol poisoning.

Also note that many bar "shots" are poured larger than 1.5 oz, and that higher-proof spirits (100 proof and above) contain more alcohol per ounce.

## How Many Glasses of Wine to Get Drunk?

With a true 5 oz pour at 12% ABV, wine follows the same math. But wine glasses are where people undercount most. A generous home or restaurant pour of 7 to 9 oz of a 14% red is closer to **2 standard drinks per glass**. Two "glasses" of wine at dinner can easily be four drinks, which for many smaller adults is right at the 0.08% line. Our post on [whether wine drunk feels different from beer drunk](/never-hungover/wine-drunk-vs-beer-drunk) covers why the experience can feel different even though the alcohol is the same.

## The Factors That Change Your Number

Your personal drink count depends on far more than body weight. These are the main factors researchers and clinicians point to.

### 1. Body size and composition

Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A larger body, and especially one with more lean muscle (which holds more water than fat), dilutes the same amount of alcohol more. That's why heavier, more muscular people tend to reach a lower BAC from the same drinks.

### 2. Sex

On average, women reach a higher BAC than men after the same number of drinks, even at the same body weight. The main reason is that women, on average, have a lower proportion of body water. Some research also suggests differences in alcohol-processing enzymes in the stomach. This is why public-health guidelines and the binge definition use lower drink counts for women.

### 3. Food in your stomach

This is one of the biggest controllable factors. Most alcohol is absorbed in the small intestine. Food, especially a meal with protein, fat, and fiber, slows the rate at which your stomach empties into the small intestine, so alcohol enters your blood more gradually and the peak BAC is lower. Drinking on an empty stomach does the opposite. We cover this in detail in our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

### 4. How fast you drink

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults, though this varies. You can't speed it up meaningfully with coffee, water, or exercise. If you drink faster than your liver clears it, alcohol builds up in your blood. Spreading four drinks over four hours produces a very different night than four drinks in one hour.

### 5. Carbonation and mixers

Some studies have found that alcohol mixed with carbonated drinks is absorbed faster for some people than the same alcohol mixed with a flat drink. The effect isn't consistent across everyone, but bubbly drinks like champagne and vodka-soda are worth treating with a little extra care. Mixing alcohol with energy drinks is a separate problem: caffeine can make you feel more alert than you are, so people tend to underestimate their intoxication and keep drinking.

### 6. Tolerance

People who drink often develop **tolerance**, meaning they feel and appear less impaired at a given BAC. This is mostly a brain adaptation, not faster processing. The important part: **tolerance does not lower your BAC.** Someone with high tolerance at 0.10% may feel fine but is still at 0.10%, still over the driving limit, and still impaired in ways they can't easily notice. Needing more drinks to feel the same effect is also a sign worth paying attention to, because it usually reflects a pattern of drinking more often.

### 7. Genetics

Genes that control alcohol-processing enzymes vary between people and populations. For example, many people of East Asian descent carry gene variants that cause acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of alcohol) to build up, leading to facial flushing, a fast heartbeat, and nausea after small amounts. That reaction is a signal from your body, not something to push through. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains it.

### 8. Medications and health conditions

Many medications, including some sleep aids, antihistamines, anxiety medications, pain medicines, and antidepressants, can add to alcohol's sedating effects or change how it's processed. Some health conditions do too. If you take any regular medication, ask your doctor or pharmacist how alcohol fits in. For some medicines, the right drink count is zero.

### 9. Sleep, stress, and illness

Being tired, sick, dehydrated, or stressed can make alcohol hit harder. Fatigue in particular adds to alcohol's effects on reaction time and judgment, so the same drinks after a sleepless week can feel very different from the same drinks after a good night's rest.

## Why You Can Feel Fine and Then Suddenly Feel Very Drunk

This is the single most important thing to understand for pacing. **Your BAC keeps rising after you stop drinking.** Alcohol takes time to move from your stomach and intestine into your blood. Depending on food and speed, BAC usually peaks somewhere between about 30 and 90 minutes after your last drink.

That delay creates a trap. You have a few drinks, feel only slightly buzzed, and have another because you "don't feel it." By the time the first drinks have fully absorbed, you've overshot. The classic signs of overshooting are suddenly feeling much drunker than you did 20 minutes ago, the room spinning when you lie down, and nausea. If that's happened to you, our post on [the drunk spins](/never-hungover/drunk-spins) explains what's going on.

The practical fix is simple: **when you notice the first buzz, slow down rather than speed up.** The buzz you feel now is the leading edge of what's still on the way.

## Tipsy vs. Drunk: The Signs to Watch For

Being able to read your own signals is more useful than any chart. Here's a simple guide.

**You're probably tipsy (around 0.03% to 0.06%) if you notice:**

- A warm, relaxed, chatty feeling
- Slightly louder voice and more confidence
- Small lapses in focus or caution
- Feeling like another drink sounds like a great idea

**You're probably past tipsy and into drunk (around 0.08% and up) if you notice:**

- Trouble with balance, bumping into things, or needing to concentrate to walk normally
- Slurred or slowed speech
- Repeating yourself or losing your train of thought
- Blurry or doubled vision
- Strong emotions that come out of nowhere
- Making choices you normally wouldn't

**You're in risky territory if:**

- The room spins when you close your eyes
- You feel nauseous or have vomited
- You're having gaps in your memory of the last hour
- Friends are asking if you're okay

At that point, the right move is to stop drinking, switch to water, eat something if you can keep it down, and make sure you have a safe way home.

## How to Pace Yourself: Practical Tips That Work

If your goal is a fun night where you stay in the pleasant "tipsy" range, these habits help. None of them are complicated.

1. **Eat a real meal before and while you drink.** This is the biggest single lever you have.
2. **Count standard drinks, not glasses.** Know your pour sizes and ABV. A double is two drinks.
3. **Aim for about one standard drink per hour or slower.** That roughly matches how fast many adults clear alcohol.
4. **Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.** A glass of water between drinks slows your pace and helps with hydration.
5. **Decide your number before you start.** It's much easier to stick to a plan you made sober.
6. **Skip shots and drinking games.** These are the fastest way to overshoot because they push lots of alcohol in quickly.
7. **Choose lower-strength drinks.** A light beer, a wine spritzer, or a lower-ABV cocktail stretches your night.
8. **Wait 20 to 30 minutes after you feel a buzz before deciding on another.** Let the delayed effect catch up.
9. **Plan your ride home in advance.** Rideshare, a designated driver, public transit, or staying over.
10. **Keep an eye on your friends, and let them keep an eye on you.**

If you notice you regularly drink more than you planned, that's worth paying attention to. Cutting back, or taking some alcohol-free nights each week, is a perfectly normal choice.

## When Getting Drunk Becomes Dangerous: Alcohol Poisoning

Alcohol poisoning happens when BAC rises so high that the parts of the brain controlling breathing, heart rate, and temperature start to shut down. It's most often caused by drinking a large amount quickly, like shots or drinking games. It is a medical emergency.

> **When to get help right away.** Call 911 (in the US) if someone who has been drinking shows any of these signs: confusion or stupor, can't be woken up, vomiting while semi-conscious, seizures, slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or gaps of 10 seconds or more between breaths, pale or bluish skin, or low body temperature. Don't wait for every sign to appear. While you wait for help, stay with the person, keep them sitting up or lying on their side (the recovery position) so they don't choke if they vomit, and don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or more alcohol. Those don't sober anyone up. You can also call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for advice.

Many people worry about getting a friend in trouble by calling for help. Many US states have "medical amnesty" or Good Samaritan laws that protect people who call for help in an alcohol emergency, and most colleges have similar policies. Getting help is always the right call. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers this in more detail.

## Myths About Getting Drunk (and Sobering Up)

**"Coffee sobers you up."** No. Caffeine may make you feel more awake, but it doesn't lower your BAC. You become a wide-awake drunk person, which can be more dangerous because you feel more capable than you are.

**"A cold shower or fresh air will sober you up."** No. These may make you feel more alert briefly, but only time lowers your BAC.

**"Beer before liquor, never been sicker."** The order doesn't matter much. The total amount of alcohol and how fast you drink it are what matter.

**"Big people can't get drunk on a few drinks."** Size helps, but a large person drinking fast on an empty stomach can still reach 0.08% surprisingly quickly.

**"If I don't feel drunk, I'm okay to drive."** No. Tolerance and the rising-BAC delay both mean you can be impaired without feeling it. If you've been drinking, don't drive.

**"Throwing up will make me sober."** Vomiting doesn't remove alcohol that's already in your blood. It's a sign you've drunk too much, not a fix.

## Getting Drunk and Hangovers: The Connection

Hangovers generally get worse as the amount you drink goes up. Studies of hangover severity tend to find that higher peak BACs are linked with worse next-day symptoms, although some people get hangovers after relatively modest amounts. Staying in the tipsy range instead of the drunk range is one of the most reliable ways to wake up feeling okay. For the full list of habits with the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where Does DHM Fit In?

Some people add a supplement to their night out. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. To be clear about what it does and doesn't do:

- **There is no good evidence that DHM keeps you from getting drunk** or meaningfully lowers your BAC in people.
- It doesn't make it safe to drive, doesn't let you drink more safely, and doesn't protect against alcohol poisoning.
- Where people find it useful is as part of a "morning after" routine alongside the basics: pacing, eating, and hydrating.

If you'd like to try it, a popular option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. No supplement replaces the most effective strategy, which is drinking less and drinking slower.

## The Bottom Line

- Most adults feel **tipsy after about 2 to 3 standard drinks** and reach **0.08% after roughly 3 to 5 standard drinks in two hours**, but your number depends on weight, sex, food, speed, tolerance, genetics, and medications.
- **Count standard drinks, not glasses.** Pints, big wine pours, strong craft beers, and cocktails often contain 2 or more drinks each.
- **BAC keeps rising after your last drink.** If you feel a buzz, slow down. More is still on the way.
- **Tolerance hides impairment but doesn't lower your BAC.**
- **Never drive after drinking**, and call 911 at the first sign of alcohol poisoning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How many drinks does it take to get drunk?**

For many adults, about 3 to 5 standard drinks in about two hours brings blood alcohol to around 0.08%, the US legal driving limit and the level most people consider drunk. Smaller people, women, and anyone drinking quickly or on an empty stomach may get there on fewer drinks. Larger people who eat and pace themselves may take more. A standard drink is 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor.

**How many drinks does it take to feel tipsy?**

Most adults start to feel tipsy, meaning relaxed, chatty, and a bit less cautious, after about 1 to 3 standard drinks, depending on body size, sex, food, and how fast they drink. This roughly corresponds to a BAC of 0.03% to 0.06%. Judgment and reaction time are already affected at this level, so it isn't safe to drive.

**How many beers does it take to get drunk?**

With regular 12 oz beers at about 5% ABV, an average-sized man may reach 0.08% after about 4 to 5 beers in two hours and an average-sized woman after about 3. Strong craft beers change this a lot: a 16 oz pint of 7% IPA is close to 2 standard drinks, so two or three pints can equal five or six regular beers.

**How many shots does it take to get drunk?**

A standard 1.5 oz shot of 80-proof liquor equals one standard drink, so roughly 3 to 5 shots in two hours brings many adults to around 0.08%. Shots are risky because they're drunk quickly and the alcohol keeps absorbing for 30 to 90 minutes afterward. People who keep taking shots because they don't feel it yet are the most likely to overshoot into vomiting, blackouts, or alcohol poisoning.

**Why do women get drunk faster than men?**

On average, women have a lower proportion of body water than men of the same weight, so the same amount of alcohol produces a higher concentration in the blood. Some research also points to differences in alcohol-processing enzymes. That's why public-health guidelines and the definition of binge drinking (4 drinks for women versus 5 for men in about two hours) use lower numbers for women.

**Does eating food stop you from getting drunk?**

Food doesn't stop you from getting drunk, but it slows how quickly alcohol enters your blood, which lowers your peak BAC and makes the effects come on more gradually. A meal with protein, fat, and fiber before and during drinking is one of the most effective ways to stay in a comfortable range. Drinking on an empty stomach does the opposite and can make the same drinks hit much harder.

**How long does it take to get drunk after drinking?**

You may start to feel alcohol within 10 to 20 minutes, but blood alcohol usually peaks about 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink, depending on food and how fast you drank. That delay is why people often feel fine and then suddenly feel very drunk. If you notice a buzz, wait 20 to 30 minutes before deciding on another drink.

**Does having a high tolerance mean you're less drunk?**

No. Tolerance means you feel and appear less impaired at a given blood alcohol level, but your BAC is the same. Someone with high tolerance at 0.10% is still over the legal driving limit and still impaired in ways they may not notice. Needing more drinks to feel the same effect is also worth paying attention to, because it usually reflects drinking more often.

**Does DHM stop you from getting drunk?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents intoxication or meaningfully lowers blood alcohol in people. It does not make it safe to drive and doesn't protect against alcohol poisoning. Research on DHM focuses mostly on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, largely in animals, with limited human data. Pacing, eating, and hydrating remain the most reliable strategies.
